_about: One guided question per vignette (asked on the game-over card; the answer goes in the player's journal), and the todo list the journal shows once the vignette is finished. Links are verified; keep the tone of a note to self.

trolley-problem.title: The Trolley Problem
trolley-problem.question: Most people would pull the lever, but wouldn't push someone off a bridge to stop the same trolley. Is there a real difference between the two? What is it?

todo.text: read where it started: Philippa Foot, “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect” (1967). The trolley is a tiny example in the middle of it
then Judith Jarvis Thomson, “The Trolley Problem” (1985), who turned it into the puzzle, and “Turning the Trolley” (2008), where she changed her mind
watch Gregory Sadler walk through Foot's cases
and Michael Sandel's first Justice lecture
look up doing vs. allowing harm in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

brain-in-a-vat.title: Brain in a Vat
brain-in-a-vat.question: If you could never, ever tell the difference, would it matter to you whether your world was real? Why?

todo.text: read the First Meditation, where Descartes imagines an evil demon feeding him a false world (the plain-English version)
then Hilary Putnam, “Brains in a Vat” (1981), chapter 1 of Reason, Truth and History. He argues you can't even coherently say it
watch Sanford Goldberg explain Putnam's argument
the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on it
and the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on content externalism and skepticism

platos-cave.title: Plato's Cave
platos-cave.question: Think of something you once believed completely and later saw differently. What was it like to turn around, and did you try to tell anyone?

todo.text: read the original: Plato, Republic, Book VII (514a–521b). It's only a few pages
watch Mahon McCann's reading of Book 7
or the short TED-Ed version
Stanford Encyclopedia on the ethics and politics of the Republic

ship-of-theseus.title: Ship of Theseus
ship-of-theseus.question: Which one was the real ship: the repaired one, or the one rebuilt from the old planks? What made you decide?

todo.text: find the original: Plutarch's Life of Theseus, section 23 (volume 1 of the Lives)
Hobbes added the second ship built from the old planks, in De Corpore (1655), part II, ch. 11
watch Jennifer Wang's Wireless Philosophy video
Stanford Encyclopedia: identity over time

grandfather-paradox.title: The Grandfather Paradox
grandfather-paradox.question: If you could go back, do you think you could change anything at all? What would stop you, or what wouldn't?

todo.text: David Lewis, “The Paradoxes of Time Travel” (1976). He says you can, and you can't, at the same time
the story it's usually traced to: René Barjavel's novel Le Voyageur imprudent (1943)
watch the Edinburgh INTROPHIL video on grandfather paradoxes
Stanford Encyclopedia: time travel

infinite-monkey.title: The Infinite Monkey Theorem
infinite-monkey.question: The monkeys typed “To be, or not to be” without meaning it. Do the words mean anything when no one meant them? Why?

todo.text: the original: Émile Borel's 1913 paper on statistical mechanics, where the typing monkeys first appear
and Arthur Eddington's version in The Nature of the Physical World (1928), ch. 4
watch Today I Found Out on the time someone actually tried it
the Wikipedia article has the actual odds

simulation-argument.title: The Simulation Argument
simulation-argument.question: If you found out for certain that you were in a simulation, would anything you care about change? What, and why?

todo.text: read the original paper: Nick Bostrom, “Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?” (2003)
watch Bostrom explain it himself
David Chalmers, Reality+ (2022), for the case that a simulated world is still real
the Wikipedia overview of the simulation hypothesis

fermi-paradox.title: The Fermi Paradox
fermi-paradox.question: Would you send the message, not knowing who, or what, might hear it? Why?

todo.text: read Eric Jones's account of the lunch where Fermi asked “Where is everybody?” (Los Alamos, 1985)
Michael Hart's 1975 paper arguing the silence means there's no one out there
watch Kurzgesagt, part 1
and part 2, the possible answers
Wikipedia keeps a long list of proposed solutions

tragedy-of-the-commons.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
tragedy-of-the-commons.question: Think of something shared in your own life: a kitchen, a road, the air. What keeps it from being used up, or what would?

todo.text: the original: William Forster Lloyd's lectures on population (1833), with the overgrazed pasture
Garrett Hardin, “The Tragedy of the Commons,” Science (1968), which made it famous
then Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990). Real communities that did agree on limits
watch an explainer on Ostrom's work
Wikipedia overview

footbridge.title: The Footbridge
footbridge.question: You'd pull a lever to save five, but would you push someone? If the two feel different, what exactly is the difference?

todo.text: read Judith Jarvis Thomson, “Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem” (1976), where the man on the bridge comes from
watch Christina Hendricks on the “fat man” case
David Edmonds, Would You Kill the Fat Man? A whole book on this one bridge
Stanford Encyclopedia: the doctrine of double effect

loop-track.title: The Loop
loop-track.question: On the loop, the plan only works because the trolley hits him. Does that make pulling the lever worse than in the ordinary case? Why?

todo.text: read Thomson, “The Trolley Problem” (1985), where the loop first appears
watch Christina Hendricks on the bystander and the loop
the 90-second version from Carneades
Stanford Encyclopedia: the doctrine of double effect

transplant.title: The Transplant Surgeon
transplant.question: Five lives for one, just like the lever. Why does nearly everyone say the surgeon mustn't? What would you point to?

todo.text: read Thomson, “Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem” (1976), where the surgeon sits next to the trolley
watch Gregory Sadler on killing and letting die
and Michael Sandel's Justice lecture, which puts the doctor and the trolley side by side
Stanford Encyclopedia: doing vs. allowing harm

ring-of-gyges.title: The Ring of Gyges
ring-of-gyges.question: If you knew for certain that nobody would ever find out, is there anything you'd do that you don't do now? What keeps you from it?

todo.text: read the original: Plato, Republic, Book II (359a–360d). Glaucon tells the story
then keep going: the rest of the Republic is Socrates trying to answer it
watch Gregory Sadler on the ring
Stanford Encyclopedia: Plato's ethics and politics in the Republic

prisoners-dilemma.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma
prisoners-dilemma.question: Talking is better for you whatever your partner does, yet trusting each other left you both better off. When have you been in a situation like this, and what did you do?

todo.text: watch Veritasium on the prisoner's dilemma and the tournaments
read Robert Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation (1984). Why tit for tat kept winning
the game started at RAND in 1950 (Flood and Dresher); Albert Tucker added the prisoners
Stanford Encyclopedia: prisoner's dilemma

newcombs-paradox.title: Newcomb's Paradox
newcombs-paradox.question: One box or two? Write down the argument for the answer you didn't choose, as strongly as you can. Does it change your mind?

todo.text: read Robert Nozick, “Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice” (1969)
watch Veritasium, who found people split 50/50
and Julia Galef on why it's a problem for rationality
Stanford Encyclopedia: causal decision theory

utility-monster.title: The Utility Monster
utility-monster.question: The monster really would be happier. What, if anything, is wrong with giving it the whole cake? What does adding up happiness leave out?

todo.text: read Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), p. 41, where the monster appears in a single paragraph
watch Learn Liberty on who decides the greater good
Stanford Encyclopedia: consequentialism
Wikipedia on the utility monster

chinese-room.title: The Chinese Room
chinese-room.question: You answered perfectly and understood nothing. What would it take for the room, or a computer, to really understand? How would you ever tell?

todo.text: read John Searle, “Minds, Brains, and Programs” (1980), and the replies printed alongside it
and Alan Turing, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” (1950), the test the room is aimed at
watch Philosophy Vibe on functionalism and the room
Stanford Encyclopedia: the Chinese room argument

monty-hall.title: The Monty Hall Problem
monty-hall.question: Before you saw the tally, did switching feel like it shouldn't matter? Try explaining why it does to someone else, without any numbers.

todo.text: watch Numberphile's Monty Hall video
find Steve Selvin's two letters in The American Statistician (1975), where it started
look up the letters Marilyn vos Savant got after her Parade column (1990). Many were from mathematicians, and they were wrong
Wikipedia has good diagrams
